ce:caption.ce:simple-para: Steps of microalgal primer design. Microalgal primer design involves identifying target region within the microalgae genome. After retrieving the sequences, alignment will be performed to identify the conserved regions, followed by primer design. Specificity of the primer will be examined using a BLAST search to avoid non-specific binding.

Examples of primer applications in microalgal study. Primers have been widely used in phylogenetic analysis, molecular biology and environment monitoring of microalgae. The molecular identification of microalgae was complemented by utilizing a phylogenetic tree generated using specific primers (Khaw et al., 2020). For molecular biology, three distinct genes, namely PsD4Des, PsD5Des and PsD8Des from Pavlova salina were isolated employing specific primer pairs (Zhou et al., 2007). Quantitative PCR with specific primer was adopted to identify and quantify harmful microalgae in the environment (Ebenezer et al., 2012).

Challenges/limitations and potential remedies in the application of microalgal primers. The application of microalgal primers encounters challenges/limitations such as primer bias, reliability and validity of deposited sequences and specificity of degenerate primers. These issues could be resolved by potential solutions such as leveraging artificial intelligence, implementing quality assurance and quality in the available databases and employing a combination of specific primers tailored to certain microalgal groups.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Microalgae are a diverse group of microorganisms that hold immense promise in various biotechnological applications. In the early stages of microalgal study, researchers primarily relied on morphological characteristics as the basis for analysis. However, the inherent limitations of these features posed constraints on the progression of microalgal research. The advent of molecular techniques has significantly shaped the comprehension of microalgae across different aspects, including the intricate molecular makeup of microalgae and systematic complexities that were once challenging to explore. A primer is a short single-stranded nucleic acid sequence that initiates DNA synthesis, particular polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The utilization of primers in molecular methods targeting microalgae has significantly contributed to the understanding of their genetics, taxonomy and functional genomics. A diverse array of molecular markers is essential in molecular methods that involved primers. These markers serve as indispensable tools for targeting specific genomic regions, facilitating a wide range of applications such as PCR, sequencing and genetic analysis. The strategic selection and use of these markers are pivotal in unlocking the full potential of primer-based molecular techniques. This chapter highlights the important role of molecular methods in microalgae, assesses the pivotal microalgal primers, provides a snapshot of the landscape of primer applications in microalgal research and emphasizes the challenges or limitations as well as future directions that shape the trajectory of this important molecular tool in understanding microalgal biology.

ce:section.ce:para: Microalgae, similar to plants, harness solar energy for biomass production through photosynthesis. They thrive in diverse aquatic environments, including polluted or unpolluted freshwater, brackish water, marine and terrestrial environments. These unicellular microorganisms encompass various species, ranging from prokaryotic cyanobacteria to eukaryotic algae, each displaying unique physiological features and biochemical characteristics. Microalgae have become the focus of extensive study due to their ecological significance and versatile applications across various industries. They play vital roles in global ecosystems by contributing to oxygen production, carbon dioxide fixation, nutrient cycling and energy flow. Beyond their ecological importance, microalgae have emerged as a promising resource for various industrial applications, including wastewater treatment, biofuel production and synthesis of valuable metabolites (Khaw et al., 2022; Tan et al., 2022).

In the pursuit of unlocking the full potential of microalgae for both environmental and industrial applications, molecular methods have become indispensable tools for researchers. Molecular methods involve the study of biological molecules at the molecular level, providing deeper comprehension of physiological, genetic and biochemical aspects. By delving into microalgae biodiversity, molecular methods aid in the discovery of novel species and the identification of potentially valuable bioactive compounds (Khaw et al., 2021; Tan, Yusoff, Khaw, Ahmad, & Shaharuddin, 2021). Moreover, the significance of molecular methods in microalgal research lies in their ability to unravel the intricate molecular mechanisms underlying key biological processes. Through the deciphering of the genetic makeup, gene expression pattern and metabolic pathway of microalgae, researchers can identify genes responsible for desirable traits, optimize cultivation conditions and develop genetically engineered strains with enhanced characteristics (Kumar et al., 2020).

Over the past decade, there has been a notable increase in microalgal research enriched with molecular methods. These studies have extensively reviewed molecular methods, particularly in the detection and identification of harmful microalgae from different water bodies (Chin et al., 2022; Gobry, Bachwenkizi, Kimambo, Ngassapa, & Kilulya, 2023). Nevertheless, there is a gap in existing reviews, as none have specifically addressed the crucial aspect of primers in molecular research related to microalgae. Kezyla et al. (2023) have reviewed the genetic markers utilized in studying the diversity and distribution of microalgae. However, their focus is limited to the metabarcoding approach on freshwater microalgae. Most importantly, unlike bacteria, there is a paucity of universal primer to be exploited in detecting microalgae in a specific and efficient manner (Khaw, Khong, Shaharuddin, & Yusoff, 2020). Hence, this book chapter aimed to explore the significance of molecular methods in advancing the understanding of microalgae, critically evaluate the primers utilized in previous studies, demonstrate the primer applications in microalgal studies and highlight the challenges/limitation as well as future direction of primers in shaping the core aspects of microalgal research. The selection of primers holds paramount importance in molecular research, serving as the starting point for DNA amplification and sequencing. Accurate and specific primers are essential for obtaining reliable data and contribute to the robustness and reproducibility of molecular analyses. Through the examination of past molecular methods, this chapter seeks to shed light on best practices and areas for improvement in molecular methods especially in primer design and selection.

Historically, conventional methods such as microscopy and physiological measurements were pivotal in microalgae research. During the period spanning the 1960s to the 1980s, taxonomic research of algae frequently utilized electron microscopy, photosynthetic pigments and various biochemical characteristics (Fawley & Fawley, 2020). While conventional experimental methods such as microscopy and biochemical analyses hugely contribute to clarifying physiological characteristics of microalgae, there are still drawbacks in microalgal systematics and nomenclature (Table 1).

Microalgae exhibit a vast diversity of species in different aquatic environments with unicellular features that either exist as separate individuals or in groups. Despite the availability of physiological and biochemical methods, morphological observations using microscopy have been considered as the gold standard to distinguish microalgal species in environmental samples, especially during harmful algal blooms. In order to explore deeper into the features and characteristics of microalgae, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) have been employed. However, the complexity of sample preparation poses challenges and may potentially alter sample properties. Addressing these challenges, atomic force microscopy (AFM) has emerged as a solution, eliminating the need for drying, metal coating or staining processes. Atomic force microscopy has proven to be versatile in assessing various sample properties, such as elasticity, viscoelasticity, adhesion and hydrophobicity. Nevertheless, AFM has its limitations. The maximum scanning area of an AFM image restricts its ability to capture the entire cell if microalgal cells exceed the maximum scanning area. Besides, the slow speed of AFM measurement results in low temporal resolution, making it challenging to track fast dynamic processes (Mišić Radić, Vukosav, Čačković, & Dulebo, 2023). The size range of algae spans from a few nanometres (nm) to several hundred of micrometres (μm), with the morphology of the latter easily observed with a microscope (Badr & Fouad, 2023). Much smaller microalgae, picoplankton such as Micromonas pusilla and Ostreococcus tauri, are often excluded from microscopic observation and indirectly become the obstacles in traditional isolation methods (using capillary tubes) resulting in the lack of extensive studies of these microalgae (Badr & Fouad, 2023). The advent of flow cytometry (FC) has enabled the direct isolation of pico-sized (˂2μm) microalgae directly from the environment. Imaging flow cytometry, which combines FC with fluorescence microscopy is more advanced and can access size distribution, detect morphological changes and assess the viability or metabolic activity of each enumerated microalgal cell, including those that are pico-sized (Lee et al., 2020). Nonetheless, most of these analyses depend on the labelling of cells using diverse markers, necessitating a time-consuming sample preparation process that may alter the natural characteristics of cells, thereby imposing additional constraints on their applicability (Abt, Gringel, Han, Neubauer, & Birkholz, 2020).

The conventional technique of morphological differentiation is frequently used to identify microalgae species. Nevertheless, this technique is unable to visualize minor morphological and physiological differences and is thus inadequate for microalgae species identification and classification (Ashour et al., 2019). The conventional morphology-based approaches by themselves are inefficient in providing robust information, both in terms of time and cost, especially when dealing with a large amount of samples that require routine examination (Otálora et al., 2023). Badr and Fouad (2023) reported that the limited number of microalgae morphological and structural features that can be found in samples from natural water bodies using conventional method could result in underestimation of the number of species and biodiversity. For instance, Badr and Fouad (2023) discovered 67 microalgae genera using molecular methods, whereas morphological-based approaches only revealed 17 unique genera. The discrepancy may be attributed to the possibility that using morphological-based approaches, certain species were overlooked since the morphological-based approaches would depend on the skills and proficiencies in identifying microalgae based on morphology (Esenkulova et al., 2020; Fawley & Fawley, 2020). Moreover, some species might undergo cell lysis either in the environment or during the culturing period of the experiment. This could lead to the release of genetic material or the species might be in a dormant phase, potentially causing overlook and discrepancies during microscopy analysis (Dzhembekova et al., 2020).

The morphology of microalgae is greatly affected by environmental factors, such as temperature, light and nutrient levels, which create impediments in identification. Nutrient levels, different phases of the life cycle and biological interactions (i.e. predation/herbivory) can impede the morphological identification of microalgae due to their phenotypic plasticity under changing environmental conditions (Badr & Fouad, 2023). Microalgae in cold conditions may exhibit changes in morphology, known as phenotypic plasticity. For example, Scenedesmus sp. demonstrated variations in spine length, with an average length of 9μm under the control condition (25°C) compared to an average of 3μm under 5°C growth condition (Fernando et al., 2023). Moreover, microalgae species bearing the same morphology do not necessarily correspond to the production of toxins (Pearson et al., 2021). In addition, some microalgae cultured in laboratories display more diverse morphologies compared to those microalgae collected from the environment, which further complicates their taxonomy when using the morphological-based approach (Badr & Fouad, 2023). Cell size and shape of microalgae that differ at different stages of their life cycles also imposed laborious effort to identify many microalgae using conventional microscopic approaches (Piasecka et al., 2019). Another drawback of morphology-based approaches in identifying microalgae is an intricate task to classify some microalgae to the species level (Fawley & Fawley, 2020). For instance, variable cell size (major distinctive feature to classify Ostreopsis into species) within the species impedes the classification of microalgae up to species level using morphological-based approaches and leads to problems of contradictory reports of their toxicity (Chomérat et al., 2020). In fact, a gradual decrease in the number of phycological taxonomists discouraged the practice of this classical approach (Fawley & Fawley, 2020). Alternative traditional methods, such as analyzing biomass biochemical composition, which involves assessing pigment or fatty acid profile offer valuable information. However, these approaches are time-consuming and primarily confirm the suitability of the biomass composition rather than identifying the specific strain (Otálora et al., 2023).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Primer-based molecular methods used in microalgae research
ce:section.ce:para: Recent strides in genomic technologies have revolutionized microalgae research (Mišić Radić et al., 2023). Particularly, primer-based molecular methods have emerged as a widely adopted surrogate for studying microalgae, contributing significantly to the understanding of microalgal biology. These molecular methods provide precise tools for exploring genetic diversity, gene expression dynamics and functional genomics. In microalgae research, genome analysis is the foremost technique providing sequence information about microalgal populations. This technique does not only identify individual genes and their arrangement, but also facilitates comparisons among genomes concerning gene arrangement and sequence similarity (Kumar et al., 2020).

The incorporation of molecular methods into phycological identification began in the 1970s with the advent of DNA manipulation tools (Ebenezer, Medlin, & Ki, 2012). Sequencing techniques, including gene amplification through polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and the Sanger method, significantly advanced molecular biology and continue to contribute to the high level taxonomic work. Polymerase chain reaction, as the cornerstone of molecular biology, enables the amplification of specific regions, thereby facilitating species identification, functional gene detection and the assessment of genetic diversity in microalgae research (Zhang et al., 2022). The introduction of automated sequencing in the late 1990s elevated DNA sequencing to a crucial tool for testing hypotheses related to species boundaries and relationships. During this period, sequences of the nuclear ribosomal RNA Internal Transcribed Spacer (ITS) regions, emerged as a tool for species delimitation and identification (Fawley & Fawley, 2020). The optimization of traditional PCR methods, coupled with the advent of high-throughput technologies, has propelled microalgae research into a new era characterized by precision and efficiency. For deepening the understanding of the molecular mechanisms governing the biosynthesis of specific genes, quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) has been employed. This common quantitative method utilizes primers or fluorescent probes to determine the number of copies of a given gene in a natural sample. It allows the study of the relative abundance of transcripts and aids in quantifying gene expression levels, which is crucial for comprehending the molecular mechanisms underlying microalgal responses to environmental stimuli (Kumar et al., 2020). Quantitative PCR has gained popularity in monitoring harmful microalgae due to its sensitivity, rapidity and cost-effectiveness, offering superior analytical sensitivity compared to the conventional microscopic diagnosis and enumeration. Recent qPCR tests can detect a few cells per litre (Pearson et al., 2021). This high sensitivity is important for detection of toxic species like Alexandrium catenella (Group I) that could be present at low cell densities (~80cells/L) in the beginning, but could proliferate to dangerous levels within a short time frame. These potent species have been associated with toxin uptake in shellfish above the FDA's regulatory limit (80μg saxitoxin per 100g of shellfish tissue) (Pearson et al., 2021).

On the other hand, microsatellite loci, or simple sequence repeats (SSRs), represent highly polymorphic DNA regions crucial for accessing genetic diversity within and among microalgal populations. These loci provide information that acts as a proxy for population structure and adaptive evolution (Sassenhagen, Erdner, Lougheed, Richlen, & Sjöqvist, 2022). Microsatellite markers can also aid in distinguishing different microalgal species or strains, which is relevant when working with closely related species (Ebenezer et al., 2012). For microsatellite loci analysis, specific primers are designed to amplify microsatellite loci and variations in the number of repeats at these loci provide information on genetic variability within microalgal populations. Sassenhagen et al. (2022) employed a microsatellite loci approach to estimate genotypic richness and the proportion of identical multi-locus genotypes in aquatic microalgal populations. At times, the molecular markers employed may have limitations for studying microalgae below the species level or may not be suitable for certain microalgae, such as cyanobacteria. Amplified fragment length polymorphism (AFLP) analysis has been used as an alternative method for studying genetic diversity in microalgae. Amplified fragment length polymorphisms distinguish unique genotypes, reveal genetic signatures for each isolate and identify cryptic species (Ebenezer et al., 2012). Random or selective primers are employed to amplify regions of the genome and the resulting patterns of amplified fragments can be used for genetic profiling and phylogenetic analysis. Although AFLPs have proven to be reliable tools in bacterial taxonomy both for the identification of species and discrimination of strains, they have been much less utilized in microalgae research. While random amplified polymorphic DNA (RAPD) and microsatellite loci approaches frequently provide valuable information, they are limited by inconsistent reproducibility and prolonged development time, respectively. In contrast, AFLP excels in addressing both challenges. It does not require prior knowledge of target sequences, uses small amounts of DNA (0.1–1ng), produces hundreds of dominant markers that are well dispersed throughout the genome and is highly reproducible (Ebenezer et al., 2012). Therefore, this technique is suitable for investigating clonal structure and efficiently developing diagnostic molecular markers for strain identification in toxic algal blooms. For identifying single nucleotide variations within microalgal genomes, single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis involving custom-designed primer sets to amplify specific regions containing SNPs can be employed. The variations are correlated with traits of interest, such as stress tolerance or lipid production, hence SNP analysis is always used to track and select desirable traits (Gu et al., 2023).

In recent years, the genomic analysis of microalgae has undergone a significant transformation, progressing from the sequencing of individual genomes to the exploration of whole genome information (culture-independent molecular method). The advance of DNA sequencing technologies, including next generation sequencing (NGS) and third generation sequencing technologies such as PacBio and Oxford Nanopore have facilitated high-throughput analysis of microalgae genomes. These NGS platforms only require DNA extraction, specific primers and bioinformatics for precise sequence recognition corresponding to each microorganism. This enables the characterization of the presence and abundance of microalgae in biological samples (Otálora et al., 2023). The insights gained from previous studies, combined with the discovery of novel proteins, provide promising targets for genetic manipulation in microalgae to enhance bioenergy applications. The information obtained fills a gap and offers better annotation of biomolecules. To decipher essential biological processes and mechanisms, transcriptomics (particularly RNA-Seq) has been employed. This NGS-based technique relies on specific primers for cDNA synthesis and amplification, enabling the quantification and characterization of the entire transcriptome in microalgae. Koh et al. (2023) employed RNA-Seq transcriptomic analysis to elucidate the molecular mechanisms governing the processes of carbon fixation and lipid accumulation in microalgae under varying carbon dioxide concentrations. The convergence of primer-based molecular techniques has opened new frontiers in microalgae research. The judicious design of primers, coupled with the high-throughput capabilities of molecular platforms, empowers researchers to delve deep into microalgae biology, paving the way for innovative applications.

Microalgae, existing either in single-celled or multicellular forms, encompass eukaryotic protists such as green microalgae (chlorophytes) and diatoms (bacillariophytes), as well as prokaryotic blue-green algae (cyanobacteria). Eukaryotic microalgae are characterized by the presence of a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, whereas prokaryotic cyanobacteria lack these structures (Andrade, Amaral, Andrade, Morioka, & Telles, 2022). To date, the number of microalgae species globally is estimated to exceed 72,500 (Fathy et al., 2023). However, only 60.7% of them have undergone formal documentation. Given the substantial number of undiscovered species awaiting identification, it becomes imperative to establish an efficient system and appropriate markers for identifying and describing microalgae. Within the realm of microalgae identification, there is a growing demand for techniques that enable efficient and precise species recognition (Fathy et al., 2023). Molecular markers, especially primers, emerged as a potent tool for distinguishing the identity of microalgae and enhancing the accuracy of taxonomic classification. Several primer pairs targeted to different genes, including 16S ribosomal DNA gene (16S rDNA), 18S ribosomal DNA gene (18S rDNA), ITS, ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase large subunit gene (rbcL), 23S ribosomal DNA gene (23S rDNA)/Universal Plastid Amplicon (UPA), elongation factor Tu gene (tuf), cytochrome oxidase I (COI) and RNA polymerase subunit (rpo) have been employed to identify microalgae (Odeh et al., 2023) (Table 2). For a primer to be deemed suitable, it must meet three essential criteria. Firstly, the ideal primer should consist of a short sequence that can be easily amplified and sequenced in one read, following a standardized laboratory protocol. Secondly, it should be flanked by a conserved region where universal primers can be placed. Finally, it must possess the capability to resolve organisms at the species level (Zimmermann, Jahn, & Gemeinholzer, 2011).

In this book chapter, the focus is placed on identifying microalgae using primers. The majority of microalgal studies aiming at the rbcL region are primarily focused on diatom metabarcoding. These studies regularly utilize a primer set targeting the rbcL region designed by Vasselon et al. (2017) for diatom identification. Another frequently used primer set was designed by Kelly et al. (2018) (rbcL 646F and rbcL 998R). Initially, this primer set was designed for adapting a DNA metabarcoding approach to assess an environment in the UK Environment Agency routine monitoring program (Kelly et al., 2018). This primer pair was subsequently utilized by another publication to evaluate rbcL for DNA metabarcoding (Seymour et al., 2020). Additionally, another study employed rbcL region primers to differentiate microalgae from the Chlorophyceae and cyanobacteria groups (Ballesteros et al., 2021).

On the other hand, the highly conserved ribosomal small subunits (SSU) 16S and 18S ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) are extensively used for the phylogenetic identification and classification of bacteria and eukaryotic organisms, respectively. The 16S rRNA and 18S rRNA are ribosomal RNA molecules found in different microalgae, specifically in the small subunit of respective ribosomes. The 16S rRNA is predominantly found in the 30S ribosomal subunit of cyanobacteria, while the 18S rRNA resides in the 40S ribosomal subunit of eukaryotic microalgae. Both types of rRNA play a pivotal role in ribosome assembly, providing a structural foundation for the binding of other ribosomal components during protein synthesis. Besides, both 16S and 18S rRNA exhibit conserved and variable regions, contributing to their significance in taxonomic classification and phylogenetic classification across different microalgal species. The 18S rRNA gene is commonly used to estimate the relative abundances and diversities of species in environmental samples due to its low intraspecific but high interspecific variation (Zimmermann et al., 2011). There are many primer pairs targeting the 18S rRNA region, with the best capability in distinguishing eukaryotes in environmental samples. The primer pair, 18S1 paired with either 18S R2 or SS3, was the most commonly employed (Duong, Li, Nowak, & Schenk, 2012). For 16S rRNA region, most primer pairs target cyanobacteria. Additional 16S rDNA primer pairs (PSF and PSR) were specifically developed to distinguish between eukaryotes and cyanobacteria (Stiller & McClanahan, 2005). However, Kezyla et al. (2023) mentioned that the 16S rRNAs region alone is challenging for simultaneously identifying both eukaryotes and cyanobacteria.

In the majority of phytogeographic studies, the ITS region has been extensively utilized. The ITS is a non-coding hypervariable domain positioned between the ribosomal subunits. In the case of eukaryotic microalgae, the ITS region consists of ITS1 and ITS2 spacers situated between the conserved 18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNA genes. Although the absence of a nuclear membrane structure in prokaryotic microalgae like cyanobacteria, their operon includes genes coding for 16S, 23S and 5S rRNA gene, each separated by an ITS (Iteman, Rippka, de Marsac, & Herdman, 2000). The notable sequence heterogeneity, and a substantial number of published 16S rRNA, 23S rRNA and ITS sequences make the rRNA-ITS highly suitable for achieving high-resolution analyses in the exploration of cyanobacterial diversity (Janse, Meima, Kardinaal, & Zwart, 2003). For eukaryotes, the ITS1 and ITS2 markers are notably recommended choices for microalgae identification. The entire ITS region is crucial for exploring differentiation between these sequences and assessing identity and similarity within two different microalgal genera. Its popularity is due to a relatively high nucleotide substitution rate, facilitating comparisons among taxa that have recently diverged. This region can be fully or partially amplified using universal primers, enabling the identification of nearly all photosynthetic organisms. Despite the high variability of ITS1 and ITS2 as markers, their primary sequences and structural characteristics can be feasibly investigated. By analyzing both nucleotide information and compensatory base fluctuations along with secondary structure information, many limitations associated with this marker can be overcome. The sufficient variability exhibited by ITS1 and ITS2 markers enables the distinction between different strains of algae. Numerous taxonomic revisions in microalgae, especially in taxa with straightforward morphology and limited ultrastructural features, have benefitted from the use of ITS1 and ITS2 as molecular markers (Fathy et al., 2023).

A segment of the chloroplast ribosomal large subunit (23S rDNA), referred to as the UPA, has been utilized for plastid-containing organisms. Primer pairs designed to target the UPA region are primarily intended for the identification of cyanobacteria and harmful microalgae, with some primers pairs aimed to identify eukaryotic diversity (Presting, 2006). However, despite its specific application, this gene has not been widely employed. It could be due to less variability of its sequence than the other markers (Hall et al., 2010; Sherwood & Presting, 2007). Less explored gene regions, such as COI, rpo and tuf, have received limited attention in microalgae research. In a study by Hall et al. (2010), COI and tuf were specifically compared with other markers to assess their effectiveness in identifying microalgae diversity (encompassing both eukaryotes and cyanobacteria). More recently, Seymour et al. (2020) conducted a test on a multi-taxa environmental DNA (eDNA) ecological assessment for freshwater phytoplankton by designing specific primer sets (m1COIintF and jgHCO2198) targeting the COI region. For rpo gene, Valério et al. (2009) developed unique primer pairs to identify cyanobacteria. However, this gene has not been utilized in any other study to date.

Some species of diatoms serve as bio-indicators for water quality monitoring of freshwater and marine ecosystems due to their rapid responses to environmental changes associated with anthropogenic activities and climate change (Visco et al., 2015). Therefore, incorporating primer-based metabarcoding or identification methods into ecological assessments is a relevant focus in modern research (Kezlya, Tseplik, & Kulikovskiy, 2023). Several primers (18S rDNA, rbcL, COI and ITS) targeting different gene regions for diatom identification have been proposed. However, each primer has its limitations: The entire18S rDNA gene does not exhibit sufficient variability; rbcL gene is less variable; COI gene is highly variable but lacks universal primers; ITS gene is variable but not universally amplifiable with standard protocols (Zimmermann et al., 2011).

The 18S rDNA gene, specifically the V4 fragment, can effectively discriminate diatoms in most cases of environmental samples, often to the species level. Its high representation in databases and ease of amplification with universal primers make it crucial for successful use in environmental studies. Although primer targets for the 18S rRNA region face challenges to resolve taxa at the species level, they are useful for environmental studies as cryptic-species complexes generally exhibit similar ecology (Zimmermann et al., 2011). For the NGS platform, the hypervariable region V4 of the 18S rRNA region is recommended due to its ease of amplification and better fits the sequencing length of Illumina Miseq (Visco et al., 2015). Although the resolution of 18S rDNA primers is lower than rbcL primers, the interspecies variation of certain primers might change between different genera and their efficiency depends on the taxonomic composition of the diatom community (Kezlya et al., 2023; Visco et al., 2015). For example, Visco et al. (2015) demonstrated that the resolution of 18S rRNA V4 region did not allow to unambiguously assign Navicula species, but it was sufficient to distinguish most of the Nitzschia and Gomphonema species from the environment sample. However, both 18S rDNA and rbcL primers are complementary, thus they should be used together in diatom studies.

In a study by Kermarrec et al. (2013), the efficiency of primers from three different target regions, including SSU rDNA, rbcL and COI were compared for compiling taxonomic inventories of mock community samples composed of diatoms. The SSU rDNA primers exhibited poor resolution at the clade and species levels. This is likely due to numerous conserved regions and low polymorphism, rendering it sensitive to sequencing errors. Despite being proposed for barcoding environmental samples, particularly for protist diversity (Zimmermann et al., 2011), SSU rDNA has limitations in intraspecies identification, especially for cryptic species (Kermarrec et al., 2013). On the other hand, the COI primer set demonstrated a high level of resolution at the intraspecies level for diatoms. However, its usage is hindered by the lower representativeness of the COI reference library. The rbcL primer pair yielded the most accurate estimation of the mock community's composition (Kermarrec et al., 2013). Although rbcL gene exhibited lower variability than COI gene within the species sampling, it proved to be a promising gene marker in brown algae, red algae and some green algae (Zimmermann et al., 2011). The use of a shorter rbcL fragment is likely efficient, given the distribution of polymorphism, ensuring informative reads at both clade and species levels (Kermarrec et al., 2013). In contrast, Kelly et al. (2018) recommended a longer rbcL region with the primer pair rbcL-646F/rbcL-998R for downstream Illumina analyses for benthic diatoms, considering taxonomic coverage, amplicon length, primer conservation and robust performance of the gene marker. Nevertheless, the rbcL gene may pose identification challenges owing to non-uniform plastid inheritance in diatoms, which can be either uniparental or biparental (Zimmermann et al., 2011).

Apart from that, a combination of the nuclear 5.8S rRNA gene and ITS2 region was proposed when screening diatoms, predominantly marine taxa of the Mediophyceae and Bacillariophyceae. The ITS region is promising for species identification and has been demonstrated in various protists, fungi and plant groups. Yet, there are challenges associated with amplifying and sequencing ITS regions using standard laboratory protocols (Zimmermann et al., 2011).

Chlorophyta represents a diverse group of eukaryotic microorganisms, comprising around 8000 identified species. However, an estimated ∼5000 species remain undiscovered, predominantly in tropical and subtropical regions. Identifying Chlorophyta can be challenging due to the lack of obvious structural features in many species, coupled with variable observable characteristics within species (Hall et al., 2010). The need for skilled experts to examine microalgal cells under a microscope is common and the existence of cryptic species and phenotypic flexibility in some species complicates clear morphological species diagnosis (Fathy et al., 2023). Hence, a primer-based molecular method targeting specific regions is crucial in identifying green microalgae.

In a study by Hall et al. (2010), the effectiveness of primers targeting 18S rRNA, COI, ITS, UPA, rbcL and tufA region across seven species groups of phylogenetically diverse green algae was assessed. The finding suggested that 18S rDNA, UPA and COI primer would be unsuitable for green algae identification because 18S rRNA and UPA genes lacking sufficient variability and COI region failed to amplify most of the taxa in this group. In contrast, the tufA gene is generally conserved and promising for species-level identification in chlorophytes. Among the tested regions, ITS, rbcL and tufA (in chlorophytes) demonstrated sufficient variability to distinguish most of the green algae species and could be amplified with relatively few primer sets. However, the rbcL fragment necessitated internal sequencing primers, thus increasing the cost of sequencing. Green microalgae, particularly within Sphaeropleales order, exhibited considerable overlap among some genera in their positions on the phylogenetic tree based on tufA gene. In addition, the position of Nephrocytium lunatum on the phylogenetic tree utilizing the tufA gene (within Chlorophyceae) was inconsistent with its classification under Trebouxiophyceae (Vieira, Bagatini, Guinart, & Vieira, 2016). Thus, none of the primers can act as universal primers that could distinguish all species. It seems likely that more than one gene may be required to meet the criteria of universality and species-level variability (Vieira et al., 2016).

The application of ITS1- and ITS2-based phylogenies has significantly reshaped the taxonomy of green microalgae. The use of ITS regions for species identification enables faster and more accurate identification of species, especially for morphologically challenging species. For instance, Fathy et al. (2023) designed primer set targeting the ITS region to differentiate between Tetraselmis and Chlorella. The findings confirmed that primer sets targeting the ITS1 and ITS2 regions effectively discriminate against the mentioned genera. A previous study suggested that ITS2 is more informative than ITS1 and 5.8S, particularly in distinguishing a wide range of Chlorophyta species (Fathy et al., 2023). The ITS2 primers resolve major green lineages, offering high resolution for taxonomic assessment, universality and the ability to distinguish most species. This makes ITS2 a useful marker for identifying unknown species, resolving conflicting identifications and expanding the use of DNA barcoding to other taxa in green algae. The ITS2 region has been successfully applied in studying the diversity of Viridiplantae, including green microalgae in the Antarctic with most taxa identified at the species level (Kezlya et al., 2023). Therefore, the ITS2 region is preferred due to its greater intraspecific variation. These studies indicate that ITS2 region has the potential to serve as a valuable DNA marker for primer design, facilitating the identification of a broad range of Chlorophyta species.

Universal 16S rDNA bacterial primers have been utilized to identify cyanobacteria and elucidated their phylogenetic relationships (Valério et al., 2005). Yet, recovery of a high number of bacterial sequences is often an obstacle in using the universal 16S rDNA bacterial primers. For instance, Stiller and McClanahan (2005) reported that utilization of the universal 16S rDNA bacterial primers identified 8 of the 11 clones as bacteria, while the rest were microalgae. Hence, Nübel et al. (1997) designed two primer sets specifically targeting cyanobacterial 16S rDNA from environmental samples (16S rDNA region). These primer sets, consisted of two forward and reverse primers, which produced amplification products ranging from 400 to 700bp. A consistent clustering of cyanobacteria in phylogenetic analysis based on the amplified gene was observed. However, these primer sets matched with several published 16S rRNA prokaryotic sequences (Nübel et al., 1997). Furthermore, these primers faced limitations in amplifying various microalgae groups due to significant mismatches in the designed primer sequences compared to the microalgae (Nübel et al., 1997).

The large ribosomal subunit (LSU) rDNA sequence comprises 12 hyper-variable domains, with the D2 domain being recognized as the most variable region, containing highly informative nucleotides in harmful microalgae. Besides, Valério et al. (2009) designed multiple primers targeting 16S rRNA, rpoC1 and the ITS region. Notably, they developed primer sets based on rpoC1 region, RPOCM61F and RPOCM624R aimed to specifically distinguish Microcystis and another primer set (RPOC145F, RPOC683R and RPOC1006R) was designed for microalgae other than Microcystis. Using these rpoC1-based primers, the study successfully identified 6 of the 38 sequenced isolates. Furthermore, the study highlighted the efficacy of cyanobacterial identification through the construction of a diagnostic key based on amplification and digestion of 16S rRNA gene amplification. In another example, the amplification and digestion of the ITS region facilitated the identification of the most common cyanobacterial species. This diagnostic key offered a rapid, easier and reliable method for identifying 15 of the 18 cyanobacterial species (Valério et al., 2009). Esenkulova et al. (2020) employed a polyphasic approach to identify phytoplankton taxa related to harmful algal blooms (HAB). Their comparison revealed that different primers exhibited diverse strengths for specific taxa, yet there was consistency in results across amplicons. Both 18S rDNA and 28S rDNA amplicons exhibited comparable outcomes and proved to be the most effective in identifying harmful algae from dinoflagellate and haptophyte groups, as well as the raphidophyte Heterosigma akashiwo. However, the 16S rDNA amplicon exclusively detected cyanobacteria but exhibited poor performance for most HAB species (Esenkulova et al., 2020).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Primers used for identification of microalgae species in natural environment
ce:section.ce:para: 16S rDNA primer is employed to identify cyanobacterial species and phototrophic eukaryotic microalgae. However, 16S rDNA primer lacks universality, particularly for heterotrophic eukaryotic species. To address the challenge of amplifying bacterial populations and targeting a diverse range of photosynthetic microorganisms such as cyanobacteria and eukaryotic microalgae, Stiller and McClanahan (2005) developed a phyto-specific (PS) 16S rDNA primer. This primer, usable as a forward or reverse primer, was combined with either a forward or reverse universal bacterial 16S rDNA primer. The primer successfully amplified both cyanobacterial and eukaryotic plastid 16S rDNA, recovering 95% eukaryotic microalgae and 5% cyanobacteria through the molecular cloning method. The high percentage of recovered eukaryotic microalgae may be attributed to their dominance in the sampling sites, including diatoms, chrysophytes and cyanobacteria. Phylogenetic analysis of the amplified gene showed consistent results with the phylogenetic analysis using the 18S rDNA gene. In a similar study, Betournay, Marsh, Donello, and Stiller (2007) utilized the PS forward primer (Stiller & McClanahan, 2005) and a reverse universal bacterial 16S rDNA primer to identify microalgae in environmental samples from three different locations. The primer successfully amplified similar microalgae groups as Stiller and McClanahan (2005) and a red algae. The primer demonstrated an 84% successful recovery rate of microalgae, albeit with some minor amplification of bacteria. However, these primers were incapable of amplifying all eukaryotic plastids, especially peridinin dinoflagellates. This is because the primer set was designed based on only 15 members of major eukaryotic algal groups and some plastid sequences did not perfectly match the primer (Stiller & McClanahan, 2005). Kezyla et al. (2023) further emphasized that the 16S rDNA primer is rarely used for the simultaneous analysis of prokaryotic and eukaryotic communities.

Presting (2006) designed universal eukaryotic plastid amplicon primers based on 37 plastid genomes from different microalgae groups and land plants. This primer targeting domain V of 23S plastid rRNA gene, resulted in approximately 400bp amplification products. Although capable of amplifying green, red, brown, diatom and cyanobacteria, the short amplified gene by UPA was deemed insufficient for effectively distinguishing all microalgal species. In the following year, Sherwood and Presting (2007) redesigned the 23S plastid rDNA primer to broaden the identification targets to multiple eukaryotic microalgal and cyanobacterial groups. This primer successfully amplified representatives from six eukaryotic algal (red, green, brown algae, diatoms, euglenoids and xanthophytes) and cyanobacterial lineages, with approximately 410bp amplified products. However, the primer failed to amplify a dinoflagellate member, Symbiodinium. Despite this limitation, the primer was recommended for screening microalgae from environmental samples. The 23S rDNA primers have been promoted as a universal identification tool for microalgae. However, lack of discriminatory power has been observed when using 23S rDNA primers for microalgae. They can only amplify a short DNA sequence (around 300–400bp), which is inadequate to distinguish microalgal species. Similarly, 18S rDNA and 28S rDNA primers, known as universal primers for microalgae, face limited universality issues as they exclude cyanobacteria from the amplification. This limitation is also applicable to the 5.8S rDNA-ITS primer as the 5.8S-ITS rRNA gene is absent in cyanobacteria, resulting in the neglect of cyanobacteria in microalgae detection (Hall et al., 2010; Kezlya et al., 2023). Moreover, the 5.8S rDNA-ITS sequence is unsuitable for differentiating diverse microalgae genera.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Unlocking precision in microalgae identification through collaborative primer combinations
ce:section.ce:para: Since there are pits and caveats of each primer, not a single primer is capable of providing universality and discriminatory power for identification of microalgae. Therefore, it becomes imperative to combine multiple primer sets to enhance the precision and coverage in the identification of microalgae. A series of studies have demonstrated the combination of primers in increasing the coverage of the microalgae and precision microalgae identification. Paradigms for these primer combinations include 16S rDNA, 23S rDNA, 18S rDNA and rbcL primers (Ballesteros et al., 2021), 18S rDNA and ITS primers (Odeh et al., 2023), 16S rDNA, 18SrDNA and rbcL primers (Badr & Fouad, 2023). For instance, Seymour et al. (2020) employed a high-throughput platform that enables rapid, high-resolution ecological assessment through eDNA. Their approach involved the utilization of multi-taxa targeting the 18S, COI and rbcL regions. In Ballesteros et al. (2021) study, dual primers were tested to identify freshwater Chlorophyceae and cyanobacteria. The results indicated that the 18S V4 hypervariable region is sufficient for distinguishing between isolates, while rbcL region is crucial for genus identification in Scenedesmaceae and Chlorellaceae strains. In cyanobacteria, both primer sets facilitated the genus-level assignment in 90% of strains. These results underscore the importance of incorporating a second primer, in addition to small ribosomal subunit sequences, to enhance molecular identification. Another recent illustration is the work of Odeh et al. (2023), who employed both ITS and 18S rDNA primers to identify Chlorophyceae in Northern Jordan. Furthermore, Badr and Fouad (2023) recommended the use of the16S rRNA V1-V3 or V4-V5 region and 18S rRNA V4 region for the identification of both cyanobacteria and eukaryotic microalgae. The 18S rDNA primer has proven its effectiveness in identifying a wide range of eukaryotic microalgae except cyanobacteria, while 16S rDNA primers serve to ‘conceal’ the limitations of the 18S rDNA primers by amplifying and identifying cyanobacteria in the field samples.

The first important step in designing microalgal primers involves identifying of a suitable genomic region as the target (Fig. 1). The commonly targeted regions for each microalga have been addressed in the previous sections. The selection of target region is crucial to ensure that the primers accurately represent and distinguish among various microalgal species. Once the target region was selected, the sequences of that region will be retrieved from International Nucleotide Sequence Databases (INSDs) such as GenBank. Then, ClustalOmega software will be utilized for multiple sequence alignments to identify conserved regions across a diverse range of microalgal species. The conserved region analysis is important to pinpoint suitable regions for primer binding that will ensure broad applicability across different species. The non-conserved regions will be replaced using the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) ambiguity codes, forming degenerated primers. Following this, primer design software (i.e. National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Primer-Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) or Primer3) will be employed to design candidate primers within the conserved region. An optimal primer normally adheres to criteria such as a length of 18–24 nucleotide bases, 40–60% of GC content and an annealing temperature above 54°C. Subsequently, a BLAST search will be conducted to verify primer specificity. The designed primers will then be synthesized and subjected to experimental validation using PCR with genomic DNA isolated from microalgae. The specificity and efficiency of primer pairs will be assessed and the PCR products will proceed to sequencing to verify the identity of the amplified regions. If necessary, the primers are refined based on experimental results, leading to an iterative process of improvement.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Applications of primers in microalgal research
ce:section.ce:para: Primers play a pivotal role in the field of phylogenetic analysis (Fig. 2). A phylogenetic tree exhibits a hierarchical arrangement of taxonomic groups. Since the late 1800s, evolutionary biology has placed significant emphasis on constructing the tree of life with the aim of clarifying the evolutionary and genealogical connections among various organisms. Microalgae are a multifarious and polyphyletic group of organisms predominantly distinguished by their absence of higher plant characteristics such as roots and leaves. Utilization of proper primers could unravel the intricate web of evolutionary relationships among microalgae. This molecular method facilitated the identification of several branching phylogenetic lineages. Many newly identified higher taxa also have been established through the phylogenetic analysis of previously described species. For example, the phylogenetic tree and ultrastructural information have unveiled that the traditionally diverse group of flagellates with organic body scales, known as Prasinophyceae, is actually a paraphyletic collection of early diverging lineages. These lineages are now being redefined as new orders or classes (Leliaert et al., 2012). Moreover, a combined examination of 18S rDNA sequences and morphological characteristics indicated sarcinoid green microalgae were reallocated to new genera, Desmotetra, Sarcinochlamys and Neochlorosarcina, alongside the existing Chlorosarcinopsis and Chlorosarcina (Watanabe, Mitsui, Nakayama, & Inouye, 2006). In other cases, phylogenetic analysis could lead to unforeseen taxonomic reassignments. For instance, coccoid Ignatius tetrasporus and Pseudocharacium americanum (previously under Chlorophycean) formed a monophyletic clade within the lineages of Ulvophyceae based on phylogenetic analysis using 18S rDNA sequence (Watanabe & Nakayama, 2007). Alternatively, the diversity of microalgae across various organisms or locations could be resolved using a phylogenetic tree. On the other hand, a phylogenetic tree constructed from DNA sequences using suitable primer pairs can serve as a supplementary tool for microalgal identification. For example, Khaw et al. (2020) utilized several phylogenetic trees to support the molecular identification of 35 different microalgae.

The role of primers in molecular biology field is indispensable. Molecular biology focuses on the study of biological processes at the molecular level, with a particular emphasis on the structure and function of biomolecules such as DNA and RNA involved in cellular processes. The application of primers has been exemplified in the isolation and characterization of genes, primarily those associated with lipid synthesis. For example, Zhou et al. (2007) employed specific primer pairs to isolate three genes, PsD4Des, PsD5Des and PsD8Des, which encode three front-end desaturases with different specificity from Pavlova salina. The functionality of these genes involving production of long chain polyunsaturated acids, was further demonstrated using yeast and higher plants. Apart from this, primers also have been utilized in revealing the genome of microalgae. Next generation sequencing (NGS), particularly whole genome sequencing (WGS) technologies enable a massively parallel analysis by yielding comprehensive genome information from biological samples at considerably lower cost. The significance of primers have been elucidated in the library preparation and sequencing process of WGS (Ebenezer et al., 2012). In some cases, whole genome shotgun libraries were generated by inserting the DNA fragments into specific vectors (i.e. pUC18). Nevertheless, there are still gaps (between 0.15% and 5%) that exist within the assembled sequenced DNA. Therefore, primer walking (also known as directed sequencing) will be adopted to close these gaps. In this approach, a primer complementary to the known sequence is designed and utilized for the initial sequencing cycle. The sequence obtained in the first cycle of sequencing is then employed to formulate a new primer, initiating a subsequent round of sequencing. These cycles are iterated until the entire sequence is obtained or until the gap is filled. Moreover, primers are essential in the context of transcriptomic studies on microalgae. Creation of a cDNA library from RNA using primers is one of the critical procedures in some of the RNA-Seq (one of NGS examples). For instance, primers have been employed in the conversion of RNA to cDNA for transcriptome sequencing, providing metabolic insight into Neochloris oleoabundans and Dunaliella parva (Rismani-Yazdi, Haznedaroglu, Hsin, & Peccia, 2012).

Specific microalgae species have the ability to synthesis harmful biotoxins that pose a threat to humans, farmed fish and aquatic living organisms. Conversely, non-toxic microalgae producers diminish the oxygen in the aquatic habitat by proliferating rapidly and covering the water surface. This will result in the devastation of aquatic organisms. Therefore, rigorous monitoring programs are essential in scrutinizing harmful microalgae species. Nucleic acid amplification techniques like qPCR, exhibit considerable potential for applications in microalgal diagnostics. Quantitative PCR is an improved version of traditional PCR, enabling the simultaneous quantification, amplification and identification of particular DNA sequences. This molecular method adopted either primer with **SYBR® Green dye or probes in detecting and quantifying the specific gene target (Ebenezer et al., 2012). Moreover, this method showed superior sensitivity compared to the classic microscopy technique. For instance, cell enumeration haemocytometer-based approach can detect a range of approximately 1000 and 10,000,000cells/L, whereas qPCR method is capable of identifying even a few cells/L (Pearson et al., 2021). On the other hand, multiplex PCR utilizes multiple pairs of primers to detect multiple targets concurrently. Specific primers designed for multiplex PCR, targeting on ITS and large subunit rDNA genes were developed to detect six harmful microalgae such as Karlodinium veneficum, Chattonella marina, Skeletonema spp., Scrippsiella trochoidea, Karenia mikimotoi and Prorocentrum donghaiense. These harmful microalgae are commonly found along the coast of China (Ebenezer et al., 2012). Furthermore, multiplex quantitative detection can be achieved by combining multiplex PCR with qPCR, which involved the usage of several primer pairs (Ebenezer et al., 2012). Apart from these, loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) is a method that utilizes four to six primers (external, internal and ring primers) for identifying harmful microalgae. A LAMP assay was devised to detect Alexandrium tamarense and A. catenina rapidly (within 20min) through direct observation of the turbidity of the amplification products (Liu, Zhang, Wang, & Chen, 2022). An enhanced version of LAMP, characterized by higher detection specificity and simplified detection procedure, was developed in conjunction with a chromatographic lateral-flow dipstick for identification of C. marina (Liu et al., 2022). On the other hand, metagenomics, an example of NGS, has exhibited the capability to monitor the microalgal diversity in aquatic environments. This technology facilitates the collection of DNA data from environments through the use of specific primers, primarily targeting the 18S rDNA gene (Ballesteros et al., 2021). The advancement of this technology has enabled the direct sequencing of numerous genomic fragments obtained from environmental samples, thereby suggesting metagenomics technology is a promising tool for monitoring microalgae in environmental samples (Medinger et al., 2010).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Challenges/limitations in application of microalgal primers
ce:section.ce:para: Ideally, a set of unique primers is required to achieve the selective and optimal amplification of the desired target sequence. Choosing suboptimal primers may result in unintended amplification or no amplification in some cases ((Fig. 3). Strategic primer design is paramount for the success of PCR, as reflected from the direct impact of primer sequences. Nevertheless, primer specificity can introduce bias in the absence of universal primers. Biases arising from the selection of primers have been documented (Klindworth et al., 2013). Furthermore, the selection of a specific primer for microalgal identification can instigate biases in the results. In addition, bias due to primer specificity can compromise molecular-based environment studies (Pinto & Raskin, 2012). The 18S rDNA gene is found universally across living organisms and well conserved within a species. Therefore, not every microalga will be sequenced, and the recovered sequences may correspond to organisms other than microalgae. Moreover, primers preferentially bind to the prevalent template in a sample, thereby concealing the rare and minor organisms (Ebenezer et al., 2012). This phenomenon was noted in a study conducted by Salmaso et al. (2022), where the entire Euglenales species was omitted when using NGS with 18S rDNA primers but was identified through light microscopy. This observation is substantiated through an in-silico PCR performed with TestPrime 1.0 (Klindworth et al., 2013), revealing a complete absence of amplification for the entire euglenoid group when employing the respective forward and reverse primers.

The design of primer heavily relies on INSDs such as GenBank, DNA Data Bank of Japan and European Molecular Biology Laboratory. GenBank is one of the primary open-access databases that encompasses nucleotide sequences of approximately 400,000 formally described species (Benson et al., 2018). Each of these databases accepts submissions of nucleotide sequences and regularly exchanges new and updated data daily to ensure optimal synchronization among them. Apart from these, DNA barcode reference libraries like Barcode of Life Data System are also pivotal for primer design. Furthermore, the design of primers also depends on more taxonomic specific reference libraries (i.e. Diat.barcode). Diat.barcode, an open-access database, has been available since 2012 and encompasses an extensive collection of diatom sequences. However, it is crucial to note that these databases and reference libraries may not include every microalga (Weigand et al., 2019). In addition, the reliability of sequences deposited in INSDs and libraries poses another obstacle in designing primers. Artificial elements created by humans such as errors in identification, sequence contamination, incomplete reference data or insufficient data can amplify the inaccuracy of the deposited sequences, leading to interference with primer design. Furthermore, the sequences available in the INSDs and libraries are originated from direct submissions from individual laboratories and batch submissions from large-scale sequencing projects (Benson et al., 2018). These sequences lack accompanying morphological data. Morphological features are essential pieces of information in assigning identity to the molecular sequences (Weigand et al., 2019). In certain instances, inconsistencies between morphological characteristics and molecular data of microalgae were observed (Khaw et al., 2020). This could result in inaccuracies in the sequences when they are deposited in INSDs and libraries, subsequently obstructing primer design.

Primer sets employed in multi template PCR should possess a sequence share among the targets. However, the targets do not share common sequences especially microalgae due to the polyphyletic nature of microalgae. In some cases, a single mismatch between a primer and particular targets typically results in very low amplification efficiency, consequently introducing a substantial bias in the amplification process. A degenerate primer, consisting of a mixture of oligonucleotides varying in base sequence corresponding to the variations among homologues, is frequently employed to prevent such bias (Bradley, Pinto, & Guest, 2016). The degeneracy of the primer refers to the number of variety sequence combinations it includes. If the degeneracy of the primer is too high, it can lead to the amplification of unrelated sequences, resulting in a loss of primer specificity. On the other hand, higher degeneracy promotes higher coverage of the primer. In the other words, a higher number of degenerate primers increases the likelihood of annealing to the target sites of interest. Hence, there is a trade-off between specificity and coverage of degenerate primer. The degree of bias in PCR amplification using degenerate primers was investigated (Polz & Cavanaugh, 1998). The findings indicated that higher primer affinity for the GC (Guanine and Cytosine) rich region than the AT (Adenine and Thymine) region due to greater binding energy between G and C than A and T. In addition, the template with a GC-rich permutation at the priming site exhibited more efficient amplification compared to the one with an AT-rich permutation. Hence, the use of degenerate primers should be examined carefully as it could introduce bias in PCR amplification.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Future development of primers in microalgae
ce:section.ce:para: In the current microalgae research-to-commercialization, the research process involves discerning the functionality and applications of microalgae. Therefore, high throughput screening and establishment of the identity of microalgae are pivotal roles for unlocking their full potential value. Screening and identifying microalgae are challenging and arduous tasks that demand a high level of expertise in both morphological and molecular identification techniques. These time-consuming processes can be addressed through the application of artificial intelligence (AI) (Fig. 3). Artificial intelligence is a multifaceted field with diverse classification and definitions. The AI algorithms can be categorized into three different classes: machine learning, metaheuristic and expert system. Machine learning such as Finite State Machine (FSM) has been established to develop efficient primers for PCR. The FSM predicts the success of amplification by a given primer pair via the fitness function. In addition, metaheuristic approaches including Genetic algorithms were applied for the exploration of unique regions in multiplex PCR primer design. Genetic algorithms are the population-based search algorithms derived from the principles of natural selection and genetics. These algorithms are frequently employed to synthesis superior solutions for optimization and search problems, leveraging biologically inspired operators like mutation, crossover and selection (Mirjalili, 2018). This approach increased the specificity of the multiplex PCR primers by preventing them from annealing in multiple locations. Moreover, a free web-based application “pcrEfficiency” (using machine learning regression model) was introduced to anticipate the PCR efficiency of quantitative PCR (Mallona, Weiss, & Egea-Cortines, 2011). Hence, this demonstrated the potential of further advancement of AI-driven efficiency prediction.

As mentioned in the earlier section, the success of primer design critically hinges on well-curated INSDs and reference libraries. The quantity of microalgal sequences submitted to these INSDs and libraries has rapidly increased. A process of quality assurance is implemented on these submitted sequences to ensure their accuracy (Benson et al., 2018). Nevertheless, erroneous sequences such as incorrect or unsatisfactory taxonomic annotations, inadequate identified sequences and lack of sequence annotations in these INSDs and reference libraries translates into a matter of concern in designing effective primers. To address these issues, two quality components, quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC) are urgently required. Quality assurance involves processes aimed at establishing and maintaining quality standards for the submitted sequences and INSDs and reference libraries. In contrast, QC focuses on users and allows for the cross-validation of taxonomic assignments or identification of questionable sequences. In the broader context, QA and QC can be viewed as internal (or preventive) and external (or reactive) curation of INSDs and reference libraries. Incorporation of QA in the development of INSDs and reference libraries is the initial crucial step for sustainable data quality management. Formally accurate sequences are deposited alongside voucher specimens, valid taxonomy and detailed metadata information. A taxonomic backbone is important for these INSDs and reference libraries, with regular updates necessary to ensure accuracy for users (Weigand et al., 2019). The prevalence of microalgae in INSDs and reference libraries lacking proper morphological identification highlights a potential need for improved taxonomy within the global microalgae community. Resolving this issue would undoubtedly require the expertise of a taxonomic specialist to encompass as many genera of microalgae as possible. At the same time, the application of QC involves scrutinizing sequence entries for potential contamination and staying updated on the latest taxonomic changes. Furthermore, supplementing the sequences in INSDs and reference libraries with their own morphological characteristics is imperative for establishing more comprehensive and reliable reference datasets (Weigand et al., 2019). Moreover, these INSDs and reference libraries could collaborate with specialized databases such as AlgaeBase to further smoothen the integrative utilization of the sequences in microalgal studies (Khaw et al., 2020). Either QA or QC alone is insufficient for meticulous maintenance of INSDs and reference libraries. So, special attention is indispensable in ensuring both QA and QC of the deposited sequences, as neglecting this aspect can restrict their applicability, render them futile, or potentially lead to inaccurate outcomes.

Since microalgae encompass a polyphyletic group, no primer pair can target all microalgae equally well. The emergence of high-throughput sequencing technologies (NGS) has made it feasible to directly investigate large scale microbial diversity. The reliability and accuracy of the analysis heavily depends on the primers, making them a crucial component in the process (Schloss, Gevers, & Westcott, 2011). The 16S rRNA gene has commonly been considered as the primary marker for exploring microbial diversity, leading numerous studies to predominantly concentrate on bacterial and archaeal groups. A plethora of universal primers have been designed using the 16S rRNA gene, yet none of them have achieved comprehensive coverage across all bacterial and archaeal groups (Klindworth et al., 2013). Similarly, the same challenge extends to microalgae and the situation in their case may be less thoroughly investigated. Two different cyanobacteria-specific 16S rDNA primers for NGS platforms were developed to increase the specificity towards cyanobacteria. This study revealed that the specificity of these primers amplifying cyanobacteria are at least three times higher compared to the universal 16S rDNA primers (Lee et al., 2017). On the other hand, metagenomics analysis of eukaryotic microalgae has been conducted by comparing the 18S rDNA gene as a key taxonomic marker (Ebenezer et al., 2012). Nevertheless, the aforementioned primers are not customarily designed specifically for eukaryotic microalgae. Moreover, the presence of multiple copies of the SSU region can significantly impact the accuracy of abundance estimates for all species when employing metagenomic platforms (Medinger et al., 2010). Addressing these challenges might be achievable by developing group-specific PCR primers in metagenomics. This approach allows for precision in targeting particular groups without inadvertently amplifying multiple copies of gene markers, thereby mitigating potential issues related to abundance estimates in metagenomics analyses. After the design of these group-specific PCR primers, it is advocated that a combination of these primers in molecular techniques especially NGS could further uncover the authentic diversity of microalgae that exist in the environment. This tailored method may ensure a more accurate and comprehensive understanding of microalgal populations.

The emergence of molecular techniques especially NGS, has significantly propelled progress in both ecological and molecular research on microalgae. This molecular breakthrough has revolutionized the microalgae field through exploring and understanding the whole genomic makeup of microalgae and intricate dynamics of microalgal communities. The primer, a short oligonucleotide is a critical component in molecular methods applied to the study of microalgae. This small but pivotal element plays a foundational role in processes such as PCR, where its design and specificity are paramount. A plethora of gene markers are available, providing a diverse array of options for primers to selectively target in molecular studies of microalgae. The versatility in gene markers not only allows for a nuanced exploration of microalgal diversity but also accommodates the diverse goals of researchers in the microalgal field. Primers have been widely utilized in a myriad of applications such as phylogenetic analysis, functional genomics and environment monitoring. While primers have significantly advanced molecular biology research, certain limitations impede their diverse applications. Nevertheless, these caveats potentially can be ameliorated through the integration of artificial intelligence, a comprehensive curated repository enriched with morphological data and high-throughput sequencing techniques employing specific markers tailored for particular groups of microalgae. Extensive collaboration and knowledge exchange within the microalgae community on primers are essential to promote and accelerate the advances in primer design and usage strategies.
